name: Median raphe nucleus
summary: The median raphe nucleus is the serotonergic nucleus of the midline pontine tegmentum, below and behind the dorsal raphe, between the medial longitudinal fasciculi and the reticular formation, with the superior central nucleus of Bechterew. Its neurons project mainly to the hippocampus, the septum, the hypothalamus and the medial cortex, where serotonin regulates hippocampal theta rhythm, memory consolidation, anxiety and stress resilience, and it acts as a brake on the dorsal raphe and the amygdala. It is part of the pontine sleep circuitry and contributes to the serotonergic modulation of breathing and of the cardiovascular reflexes, and its damage in pontine strokes and in neurodegeneration adds anxiety, memory impairment and sleep disturbance to the classical signs.

anatomy.location: Midline of the rostral pontine tegmentum in the paramedian reticular formation, below the dorsal raphe and the aqueduct-fourth ventricle junction, above the pontine nuclei and the basis pontis, between the medial longitudinal fasciculi and lateral to the midline seam.

function: Median raphe serotonergic neurons reach the hippocampus and septal area through the medial forebrain bundle and the fornix and desynchronize hippocampal theta, tuning memory encoding and acting as a resilience system that damps the response to stress and fear; they inhibit the amygdala and the dorsal raphe, which are more anxiogenic, and project to the suprachiasmatic nucleus to modulate circadian entrainment. Together with the medullary raphe they modulate the respiratory chemoreflex and sympathetic tone, and their activity across the sleep-wake cycle mirrors the dorsal raphe. The nucleus receives the prefrontal cortex, the lateral habenula and the hypothalamus.

imaging.normalAppearance: The midline of the rostral pontine tegmentum on axial images, in front of the fourth ventricle and behind the basis pontis; not resolved as a discrete nucleus.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the paramedian pontine tegmentum with gaze palsy, internuclear ophthalmoplegia and often mood and sleep change.
Symmetric central pontine T2 hyperintensity sparing the periphery after rapid sodium correction, with pseudobulbar signs and altered behavior.

pathology.pathology: Multiple system atrophy or Parkinson disease (functional)
pathology.finding: Reduced serotonergic markers in the pontine raphe on PET associated with anxiety, sleep and autonomic symptoms.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of median raphe serotonergic damping of the amygdala and hippocampus
Loss of serotonergic modulation of hippocampal theta
Loss of raphe input to the suprachiasmatic nucleus and sleep circuits

examination: Anxiety and mood assessment in pontine lesions
pearls: Two raphe nuclei, two temperaments: the dorsal raphe arouses and the median raphe calms
The median raphe reaches the hippocampus; the dorsal raphe reaches the cortex and striatum
Central pontine myelinolysis sits exactly where the median raphe lives; behavioral change is part of it

pitfalls: Behavioral change after a pontine stroke is usually attributed to the situation; the raphe and locus coeruleus are often part of the lesion
